items.title: Repeating a measurement reduces one kind of error but not another
items.claim: Measure a length with a ruler 10 times and average — the result is more reliable than any single measurement. Measure with an uncalibrated ruler 10,000 times and the average is still wrong.
items.prompt: Why does averaging help with random error but not systematic error?

options.text: Random errors fluctuate around the true value and partially cancel when averaged (uncertainty falls as 1/√N). Systematic errors shift every measurement in the same direction by the same amount — averaging does nothing
Systematic errors are smaller than random errors

items.reveal:
Random error: unpredictable fluctuations around the true value. Sources: meniscus reading, parallax, sensor noise, vibration. Averaging N independent measurements reduces the standard error by a factor of √N.

Systematic error: every measurement shifted by the same amount in the same direction. Sources: uncalibrated instrument, zero offset, observer bias, faulty technique. Averaging doesn't help.

Good practice: repeat measurements to reduce random error, then calibrate against a known standard to detect systematic error. Report both. Modern lab work distinguishes 'repeatability' (one operator, one instrument, same day) from 'reproducibility' (different operators, different instruments, different days) — they catch different sources of error.
items.why: Students take averages without thinking about which errors averaging can and cannot fix. Real precision needs different techniques for different error types.

items.title: Significant figures are a sloppy short-hand for uncertainty
items.claim: Quoting a length as 3.14 m suggests it lies between 3.135 m and 3.145 m. Quoting it as 3.140 m narrows that to 3.1395 to 3.1405. Significant figures encode uncertainty but only approximately and discontinuously.
items.prompt: What does a precise measurement actually look like?

options.text: A central value with an explicit uncertainty: 3.140 ± 0.002 m. This makes the precision claim mathematically clear and propagates through subsequent calculations
Calibrated against a known unit only

items.reveal:
Significant figures are a quick shorthand. Real precision quotes uncertainty explicitly: 3.140 ± 0.002 m, or with a percentage (3.140 m ± 0.06 percent), or with a confidence interval (e.g. '95 percent confidence').

When combining measurements, uncertainties combine: addition/subtraction adds absolute uncertainties in quadrature; multiplication/division adds relative uncertainties in quadrature.

Resolution (the smallest difference an instrument can distinguish — often the smallest division on a scale) is not the same as uncertainty. A ruler with 1 mm markings has 1 mm resolution but its uncertainty in a typical reading might be ±0.5 mm at best — and worse if it's bent or warped.
items.why: Sig figs are taught as a rounding rule. They are a coarse encoding of precision; explicit ± uncertainty is the professional approach.

items.title: The laws of physics don't tell time which way to run
items.claim: Newton's laws, Maxwell's equations and the Schrödinger equation all look the same if you reverse time. So why do we remember the past but not the future, and why does milk mix into coffee but never unmix?
items.prompt: Where does the arrow of time come from?

options.text: Gravity defines a preferred time direction
The second law of thermodynamics — entropy increases with time, statistically — but only because the universe started in an extremely low-entropy state and is far from equilibrium
Time has a built-in direction physicists haven't found yet
We perceive time directionally; physics doesn't have a preferred direction

items.reveal_title: Boltzmann's H-theorem and the low-entropy past
items.reveal:
Microscopic laws are time-reversible. But there are vastly more disordered configurations than ordered ones. Starting from any low-entropy state, the overwhelmingly likely evolution is toward higher entropy.

The question becomes: why did the universe start in such a low-entropy state? The Big Bang and the smoothness of the early universe set up an enormous entropy 'budget' that has been depleting ever since.

We remember the past because forming a memory increases entropy. We can't 'remember' the future because that would correspond to entropy decreasing in the brain.

The 'arrow of time' is an emergent statistical property of an initial condition — not a fundamental law.
items.why: Time feels like it has an obvious direction. Physically, that direction is a cosmological accident, not a fundamental property of time itself.
